The good development of the operating business is further reflected by the net interest income (EUR 274.5 million or +1.4%) and net fee and commission income (EUR 123.5 million or +10.1%). Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich has also been able to maintain its stable course in terms of capital resources. The Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio rose to 19.6% (+0.3 percentage points compared with 31 December 2025), whilst the total capital ratio rose to 21.1% (+0.1 percentage points). A conservative approach was adopted with regard to the alloca-tion of profits during the financial year for the first half of 2026. If the full interim result had been taken into account, the CET1 ratio as at 30 June 2026 would have stood at 20.6% and the total capital ratio at 22.1%. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich’s consolidated total assets increased somewhat compared with the end of 2025 and remained high at the end of June 2026 at EUR 49.2 billion. Operating profit is EUR 879.0 million, while pre-tax profit for the period amounts to EUR 846.8 million. After taking into account taxes on income and earnings and other comprehensive income (OCI), the total result for the period in the first half of 2026 is EUR 833.2 million. A key factor behind the excellent results for the first half of 2026 was the contribution to earnings from companies ac-counted for using the equity method, which generated a result of EUR 706.6 million. In the first half of 2026, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich implemented key strategic initiatives to strengthen its market position and further develop forward-looking business areas. A key milestone in the first half of 2026, and also in the history of Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich, is the start of construction of the new Group headquarters in Linz’s Neustadt district, which is being realised as one of the most signifi-cant timber construction projects in an urban setting in Austria. The ground-breaking ceremony in May 2026 marked the start of a forward-looking flagship project for sustainable construction, innovative working environments and modern urban development. The eight-storey building is being constructed using a resource-efficient hybrid timber construction method and comprises around 25,000 m² of usable floor space. A total of around 12,640 solid cubic metres of PEFC-certified timber, predominantly sourced locally, is being used in the process – a clear commitment to regional value creation and the sustainable use of natural resources. The new headquarters will in future accommodate up to 1,000 staff and feature around 750 flexibly configurable work-stations as well as spacious customer and meeting areas. The usage concept is complemented by areas open to the public, such as catering and event spaces, as well as additional green spaces and communal areas. The architecture and use of the space are based on an open, urban concept designed to make the site specifically accessible to customers and the public and to act as a catalyst for the development of the entire neighbourhood. CRR III has applied directly in all Member States since 1 January 2025, while the entry into force of the market risk regulations (Fundamental Review of the Trading Book) has been postponed to 1 January 2027. With CRD VI, the EU has fundamentally revised the regulatory requirements for credit institutions in several areas. As a directive, this should have been transposed into national law (in particular in the Austrian Banking Act, BWG) by 11 Janu-ary 2026. The draft transposition legislation is currently under review and provides for amendments and clarifications in the following areas, amongst others: fit and proper requirements, new notification obligations and supervisory powers relating to “prudentially relevant transactions”, and the treatment of ESG risks. Following the amendment to the definition of a provider of ancillary services under CRR III, the EBA published guidelines on 9 January 2026 setting out the criteria for determining the activities referred to in Article 4(1)(18) of the CRR. On 13 February 2026, the EBA issued guidelines on proportionate retail diversification methods in accordance with Article 123(1) of the CRR. The FMA has issued a positive compliance statement in respect of both guidelines. The CRR hard test for residential property (including commercial residential property) was initially extended by the FMA at least until the analysis of the reporting data as at 31 December 2025 and, in the absence of any information to the contrary, therefore remains in force (the hard test is particularly relevant in connection with own funds requirements for credit risk and under the large exposure regime). In line with this recommendation, it is envisaged that this will be increased to 2% from 1 July 2026 and to 3.5% from 1 July 2027. The relevant FMA regulation amending the Capital Buffer Regulation (KP-V) 2025 was published in the Federal Law Gazette on 23 June 2026. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/440, published on 3 June 2026, introduces amendments to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/63 supplementing the Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive (BRRD), which sets out in more detail the calculation and reporting of contributions to the EU bank levy. On the fund legislation package (transposition of AIFMD II and the UCITS Directive review): Member States had until 16 April 2026 to transpose Directive (EU) 2024/927 on the introduction of mandatory liquidity management tools to strengthening investor protection and contain systemic risk in periods of market stress. The legislative package was referred to the Finance Committee by the National Council in plenary session on 20 May 2026 and was discussed at the committee meeting on 23 June 2026. Key elements of the national transposition, which will help to strengthen the competitiveness of Austrian companies and ensure a level playing field with other European countries, are: a reduction in the minimum free-float threshold to 10% and the removal of disclosure requirements; raising the thresholds for the prospectus requirement for investment schemes and securities from EUR 5 million to EUR 12 million; introducing a re-quirement for investment prospectuses to be approved by the FMA from 2027; raising the notification threshold for man-agers’ transactions under the EU Regulation from EUR 5,000 to EUR 20,000 per calendar year. Sustainable finance At the end of 2025, a political agreement was reached at EU level on the Omnibus I package to simplify sustainability reporting (CSRD) and corporate due diligence obligations (CSDDD, also known as the EU Supply Chain Directive). The aim is to reduce the reporting burden and, in particular, to ease the burden on smaller businesses. Following its adoption by the European Parliament in December 2025 and formal approval by the Council at the end of February 2026, Legislative Act (EU) 2026/470 was published in the Official Journal on 26 February 2026 and entered into force on 18 March 2026. Member States must transpose the amendments to the CSRD by 19 March 2027 (for the CSDDD, longer deadlines apply until 26 July 2028, with the new rules coming into force in July 2029). Against this background, the Sustainability Reporting Act (NaBeG), which was only published in the Federal Law Gazette on 18 March 2026 and transposes the CSRD into national law, must be amended accordingly by 19 March 2027. A national “single entry point” is intended to consolidate and simplify reporting obligations relating to cyber and data incidents across various EU legal acts Interim Financial Report 2026 13 The Group Group interim management report 2026 | Business development and the economic situation The Group Interim Financial Report 2026 | Business development and the economic situation 13 so that businesses can submit and retrieve all reports via a central interface (including under DORA, NIS2, the RKE Directive, the GDPR and the elDAS Regulation). In early June 2026, the European supervisory authorities (EBA, EIOPA and ESMA) published their first annual report on serious ICT incidents in the EU financial sector, based on a reporting mechanism established under DORA. The report noted that ICT risks are increasingly cross-border in nature and interlinked. The latest developments in high-performance AI-powered tools should prompt financial institutions to strengthen their cybersecurity measures in order to ensure their resilience in the future. The European Commission has recently launched two consultations on the revision of the Regulation on Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) in accordance with its obligation to evaluate the regulation. The focused consultation to assess whether the regulation remains appropriate since it came into force is aimed at a rather specialised audience (e.g. providers of crypto-assets) and public authorities. In addition, the public consultation is intended to gauge the general level of knowledge, experience and views regarding the various types of digital assets and the associated services. The Commis-sion is scheduled to adopt the proposal in the fourth quarter of 2026. Tax law The Budget Consolidation Measures Act 2025 (Federal Law Gazette I No. 7/2025) introduced a decision to substantially increase the stability fee on banks. The percentages of the current stability fee were increased by around a third, and a considerable special payment was also standardised for 2025 and 2026. The special payment for 2026 must be paid in full by 31 October 2026 at the latest. The draft Budget Accompanying Act 2027–2028 provides for the extension of the stability fee increase for a further three years. The 2024 minimum tax report (GloBE Information Return, GIR 2024) had to be filed for the first time by 30 June 2026 under the Federal Act to Ensure a Global Minimum Level of Taxation for Groups of Companies (Minimum Taxation Act, MinBestG). This act is based on Council Directive (EU) 2022/2523, which in turn implements the OECD’s GloBE Model Rules. The minimum tax report is the key annual tax return under the global minimum taxation regime (the OECD’s Global Anti-Base Erosion Rules, or GloBE rules, Pillar 2). The aim of the global minimum tax is, in general, to ensure that multi-national corporate groups with a consolidated turnover of at least EUR 750 million worldwide are subject to an effective tax rate of at least 15%. AML/sanctions The EU’s new regulation on anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AMLR) will apply from 10 July 2027. Member States must also implement the fundamentals of the 6th Money Laundering Directive by the same date. The AMLA Regulation (Regulation establishing the European Anti-Money Laundering Authority) has applied since 1 July 2025, the date on which AMLA officially commenced operations. With effect from 1 January 2026, AMLA has taken over responsibility from the EBA for drafting the AML Level 2 texts. AMLA will begin direct supervision of selected banks on 1 January 2028. To identify provisionally eligible obliged entities, AMLA recently published a reporting package consisting of a standardised reporting template and an interpretative note providing specifications and instructions to national super-visory authorities. The national supervisory authorities will collect the data by 15 August 2026. The provisional list of eligible companies subject to the requirement is expected to be finalised by the end of September 2026. In future, beneficial ownership will be defined as ownership above a participation threshold of 25%; this will also apply to the underlying, indirect participation levels in future. Rules on PEP (politically exposed persons) will also be tightened. In future, all members of a state parliament and local councillors, city councillors and mayors of cities with more than 50,000 inhabitants will also be considered politically exposed persons. The obligations to update customer data will also be tight-ened. Cash payments in the commercial sector will in future be capped at EUR 10 thousand, with the exception of trans-actions between private individuals. On 23 April 2026, the Council adopted the 20th package of sanctions, which contains new restrictive measures against Russia and Belarus. These new measures include, in particular, the addition of further individuals, organisations and entities to the list, the extension of import and export bans, and the first-ever activation of the instrument to combat cir-cumvention. It also includes measures relating to the crypto sector and is aimed at the financial services sector. The FATF (Financial Action Task Force) conducts country audits at regular intervals to ensure Member State compliance with AML and CTF standards. These audits typically focus on compliance by national authorities and reporting offices. Austria’s country audit began in October 2024. The FATF country report on Austria was published on 30 April 2026. MATERIAL RISKS AND UNCERTAINTIES The long-term success of Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group is largely dependent upon active risk management. In order to achieve this target, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich, as the dominant group company, has implemented risk management with structures that facilitate the identification and measurement of all risks in the Group in accordance with sections 39, 39a, Austrian Banking Act and the Credit Institution Risk Management Regulation (KI-RMV) (credit risks, equity risks, liquidity risks, market risks, macroeconomic risks, operational risks and other risks) and their active managerial counteraction. Credit, investment and operational risk are managed by RMKM (Risk Management Credit, Reporting, Op-erational Risk), while liquidity, market and macroeconomic risk are managed by RMIM (Risk Management ICAAP & Market Risk). ESG (environment, social, governance) risks, as the latest dimension of risks, were integrated into the existing risk categories, with the greatest focus remaining on climate and environmental risks – in part because social and governance risks have not been classified as material. The overall risk strategy approved by the Managing Board ensures that the risks assumed by the Bank are consistent with the corporate strategy. The Managing Board and the Supervisory Board are regularly given reports about the risk situation. For more detailed information on the overall financial risks in the Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group in the first half of 2026 and the objectives and methods of risk management, please refer to Note “7. Risk report” in the notes to the consolidated financial statements. Macroeconomic influences and credit risk developments A year ago, this section anticipated a marked economic recovery, but while this still appears to be under way, it now looks set to be significantly slower and weaker than hoped – not least because of the Iran conflict. The ECB’s interest rate rises, both those that have already taken place and those still expected this year, are dampening an already very weak appetite for investment. In the first half of 2026, credit risk – when considering only specific allowances and provisions – was approximately on a par with the corresponding period of the previous year. The positive impact of the release of portfolio provisions was less pronounced than in the first half of 2025, particularly as ongoing conflicts, lacklustre expenditure-side budgetary measures and rising interest rates are weighing on economic prospects. Insolvency figures amongst corporate clients in the key markets of Austria and Southern Germany remain high, and further difficulties are to be expected given the bleak outlook for German car manufacturers, particularly as many suppliers in these key regions are directly or indirectly dependent on them. Despite the decidedly adverse circumstances, the Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group has managed to keep its NPL ratio well below 6%, and a further decrease below the 5% mark is forecast for the end of 2026, particularly as a number of larger non-performing real estate loans are on the verge of being realised or returning to performing status. An application has now been submitted to the ECB, with effect from 29 May 2026, to apply the Internal Ratings-Based Approach (IRB Approach) to all corporate customer financing at Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich. This results in risk-adequate capital requirements – put simply, loans to customers with top credit ratings require less capital to underpin them than loans to companies with weaker credit ratings. Once this application has been approved, it should therefore be pos-sible to offer significantly more competitive financing terms, particularly to customers with a strong credit rating, which will lead to a further improvement in portfolio quality in the medium term. Another side effect of the approval would be an increase in the already substantial capital buffer. In addition to the analysis of customs duties carried out last year, efforts were also made in the first half of 2026, in consultation with the customers affected, to quantify the impact of the war in Iran on the portfolio. The results show that the effects have so far been fairly manageable for the vast majority of customers. However, the consequences of a pro-longed blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and the resulting sustained rise in oil and gas prices would act as further brakes on economic growth and would likely cause corporate default rates to rise even further. OUTLOOK Building on its solid capital base, its high level of financial stability and its sustained successful growth trajectory, Raiff-eisenlandesbank Oberösterreich aims to further strengthen its strong market position in the Austrian banking sector. With its “IMPULS 2030” strategy, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich has developed a clear roadmap for the future, and the associated initiatives are being implemented on an ongoing basis. One key objective in this regard is to consistently consolidate and expand its position as a leading corporate bank. The focus is on entrepreneurial thinking and action, customer focus and the consistent further development of the business model. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich con-tinues to tailor its activities to clearly defined customer segments and focuses on bespoke solutions, excellent advisory services and the swift resolution of customer enquiries. An efficient, modular and market-oriented operating model supplies the necessary foundation. Through close cooperation with businesses, institutions and partners, as well as through its strong network of equity in-vestments, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich is driving economic development in its home market. A strong focus lies on the continued digitalisation and data-driven management of customer business. This involves developing a compre-hensive customer profile that brings together information on risk, needs and returns and is supplemented by modern CRM solutions. Clear standards, data-driven activity management and hybrid support models that combine personal contact with digital and scalable service approaches strengthen sales performance in the long term. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich is working to further develop its range of products and services in line with its stra-tegic priorities. These include, in particular, the expansion of ESG-focused solutions, the further development of interna-tional business and the expansion of payment services and other services. Through close cooperation within the Austrian Raiffeisen sector and with specialist partners, the Bank aims to create added value in selected business areas and expand its range of services. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich is already making targeted use of the potential offered by artificial intelligence to further develop its business and operational processes and will continue to step up these efforts in the future. By develop-ing its own AI strategy, the Bank has laid the groundwork for systematically identifying areas of application and embedding AI in a sustainable manner across relevant areas. The focus is on improving efficiency and data quality, supporting data-driven decision-making and further enhancing customer service and sales. Furthermore, the use of AI helps to identify and manage risks at an early stage while also supporting the analysis and creation of digital content. Artificial intelligence thus makes a significant contribution to achieving the Bank’s strategic objectives and to strengthening its long-term viability. In addition to traditional loan financing, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich will continue to prioritise the provision of equity capital as a key component of its range of services. The equity investment companies are not merely providers of capital; they also work alongside businesses as active partners, drawing on their extensive expertise in areas such as corporate development, management accounting, liquidity management, transformation and restructuring. Furthermore, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich relies on forward-looking liquidity management, comprehensive risk management and consistently data-driven corporate management. Through the ongoing development of processes, digital capabilities and technological solutions, the Bank is laying the foundations to continue strengthening the trust of its cus-tomers in the future. This ensures that it remains a reliable partner for businesses, institutions and private customers and enables it to provide comprehensive support for their investment, growth and future projects. Company valuations Company valuations are required both in order to determine the fair value of investments or investment instruments meas-ured at fair value as well as for impairment tests for investments accounted for using the equity method and goodwill. The main uncertainties in the first half of 2026 stemmed from the geopolitical situation, in particular the ongoing uncertain-ties surrounding trade policy and the impact of the Middle East conflict on the markets and sectors affected. The slight upward trend in economic output in Austria, which had already become apparent in 2025, continued into the start of 2026. Gross domestic product grew by 0.2% in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the fourth quarter of 2025. Industrial activity in Austria and Germany remained subdued in the first half of 2026. New orders continued to be affected by geopolitical uncertainties and rising energy costs. Given the already subdued propensity to invest, the ECB’s interest rate rise in June 2026 – prompted by rising inflationary pressures – is likely to reinforce companies’ cautious approach to investment, their focus on efficiency and their heightened cost discipline. The special fund for infrastructure and climate neutrality in Ger-many is in turn expected to constitute a driving force when it comes to investment activity. The residential property market in Austria and Germany is currently undergoing a moderate recovery. The market envi-ronment in the commercial property sector remains challenging in light of the weak industrial economy and reluctance to invest. Companies actively incorporate ESG-related risks into their strategic and operational planning, particularly in the context of CSRD, the EU Taxonomy and other EU regulatory frameworks, while risks already embedded in the business model are not disclosed separately. Each of the factors mentioned were analysed individually for each company and, where material, reflected in the cash flows underlying the valuation. Double counting of uncertainties in both cash flows and interest rates was avoided. Potential medium- to long-term impairments are evaluated through continuous risk analysis. Several important discretionary decisions are required for measuring expected credit loss, such as: defining criteria for a significant increase in the credit risk, selecting suitable models and assumptions, defining the number and relative weighting of future-oriented scenarios, defining groups of similar financial assets. The tentative economic recovery is being shaped by the impact of the war in the Middle East. Austria’s economy is particularly feeling the effects of the sharp rise in crude oil prices, which – following a positive start to the year – will lead to a noticeable slowdown in growth in the second half of the year. The OeNB identifies the required fiscal consolidation as another factor restraining growth. Despite considerable consolidation, the budget balance is improving only marginally and is being offset by proac-tive measures (such as reducing ancillary wage costs). Austrian HCPI inflation is expected to remain at 3.6% in 2025, remaining above the ECB’s medium-term target of 2%. Owing to a further energy price shock resulting from the war in the Middle East, the OeNB forecasts an annual HCPI growth rate of 3.2% for 2026. It is only in the following two years that the figure will move closer to the ECB’s medium-term target of 2.4% (2027) and 2.1% (2028). Gross domestic product is projected to grow at 1.1% and 1.2% for 2027 and 2028 respectively, with the rates therefore expected to be slightly above potential growth overall, according to the OeNB. However, this gradual acceleration in economic growth is underpinned by commodity prices returning to normal levels. Following a rise in unemployment in 2024 and 2025, the labour market is currently proving resilient in the face of the current economic climate. According to Eurostat, the unemployment rate is set to remain at 5.7% in 2026 – a level comparable to that of the previous year – and is expected to fall slightly in subsequent years. The expected credit losses developed as follows in the first half of 2026: In the first half of 2026, the expected credit loss for Stage 1 and Stage 2 declined by 4,1 % within the Raiffeisenlandes-bank Oberösterreich Group. The reduction in portfolio provisions is primarily due to portfolio improvements and more moderate IFRS 9 risk parameters, as former PD drivers (such as high HCPI growth rates) have gradually been excluded from the calculation basis due to the structure of the model. The collective stage transfer for the “Automotive” and “Mechanical engineering and plant construction” industries, ap-proved by the Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Managing Board on 31 December 2024, continues to be applied. Customers from the affected industries were collectively transferred to Stage 2. In accordance with IFRS 9, an increased portfolio provision is recognised for these customer groups by recognising the lifetime expected loss instead of the one-year expected loss as a portfolio provision. These measures led to an overall increase of around EUR 11.6 million in the Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group’s portfolio provision at 30 June 2026, measured as the difference be-tween lifetime expected loss and One Year expected loss (31 December 2025: EUR 11.0 million). RBI is the central institution in the Raiffeisen Banking Group Austria and considers Austria, together with Central and Eastern Europe (CEE), to be its home market. In Austria, the RBI is a leading corporate and investment bank and forms part of the largest banking group in the country. In Central and Eastern Europe (CEE), the RBI acts as a universal bank via its subsidiary banks and is one of the largest financial services providers in the region. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group exerts a significant influence on this investment because the Chief Executive Officer of Raiffeisen-landesbank Oberösterreich, Reinhard Schwendtbauer, is a member of the RBI Supervisory Board and as Deputy Chair-man of the Supervisory Board is an active participant in the strategic decisions made. The impact of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine remained a key challenge for RBI in the first half of 2026. Potential transactions that could lead to the deconsolidation of the Russian entity were thoroughly reviewed and monitored. RBI has significantly scaled back its operations in Russia since the start of the war and has implemented extensive measures aimed at minimising the risks associated with tougher sanctions and compliance requirements. Efforts continued in the first half of 2026 aimed at ensuring a reduction in business with Russia in line with the ECB’s guidelines. The volume of lending in local currency has fallen by 80% since the start of the war. In September 2024, a Russian court issued a temporary injunction restricting the disposal of all shares in AO Raiffeisen-bank (Network Bank Russia) with immediate effect. A transfer of the shares in AO Raiffeisenbank was not possible as a result of this decision. The decision is related to the legal proceedings initiated by Rasperia Trading Limited (“Rasperia”) against STRABAG SE, its Austrian core shareholders and AO Raiffeisenbank. Taking into account expected compensa-tion claims, AO Raiffeisenbank recognised a provision of EUR 840 million in the fourth quarter of 2024, which was reflected in this amount in RBI’s consolidated financial statements. In January 2025, a Russian court ruled that STRABAG SE and its Austrian core shareholders must pay EUR 2,044 million to Rasperia and that the judgement can be enforced against assets of AO Raiffeisenbank. In April 2025, the Russian central bank executed a judgement in favour of Rasperia in the amount of EUR 1,870 million. EUR 239 million in accrued interest was enforced in May 2025 and a further EUR 0.4 million in July 2025. In June 2025, Rasperia filed an application with the Russian court for an anti-suit injunction involving RBI. Due to the adjusted risk assessment by the RBI Managing Board, AO Raiffeisenbank recognised the expected proceeds from the enforcement of claims against Rasperia in the amount of EUR 1,204 million in the second quarter of 2025. In August 2025, a Russian court lifted the restriction on the disposal of the shares in AO Raiffeisenbank on the grounds that the payment of damages also meant that there was no longer any reason to prohibit the sale. AO Raiffeisenbank subse-quently faced a further claim for damages brought by Rasperia. A provision of EUR 339 million was set aside in the fourth quarter of 2025 following the court’s ruling. EUR 326 million (corresponding to the damages awarded, excluding interest) was enforced in March 2026 by the Russian Central Bank in favour of Rasperia. RBI announced on 23 July 2026 that, in full compliance with EU sanctions law, it had filed a claim in Austria against Rasperia for approx. EUR 3.15 billion in order to obtain damages and to enforce a judgement against Rasperia’s assets in Austria, the latter to take place once Rasperia’s frozen Austrian assets have been released. These assets, which have been frozen as a result of EU sanctions, consist of 28.5 million STRABAG shares, as well as dividends for the financial years from 2021 onwards and a cash distribution arising from STRABAG’s capital reduction in March 2024. AO Raiffeisen-bank will be the second claimant in the Austrian proceedings. The lawsuit was brought on 30 July 2026. The carrying amount of the investment in the RBI Group was subjected to a test for a reversal of impairment at the reporting date of 30 June 2026 due to a sharp rise in the share price. The fair value less sales costs as at 30 June 2026 was determined to be EUR 55.85 per share, based on the stock exchange rate of RBI on the Vienna Stock Exchange (31 De-cember 2025: EUR 38.30 per share). The value in use is determined on the basis of an external company valuation. The company valuation was calculated based on the present value of the cash flow to be expected (discounted cash flow procedure) of the companies in the Group taking into account the adjustments required for the purpose of calculating the value in use. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich analysed the planning assumptions in great detail and made more conservative assumptions regarding the Russian business and the development of the core business compared to the management of RBI and concerning the calculated enterprise value. In order to take into account the effects of the war in Russia and Ukraine, a method based on the dual control approach was used to determine the value in use. The total value of the RBI Group is made up of two components: core business (RBI Group excluding Russia) and the Russian network bank. The effects of possible spin-off and sale options with regard to the Russian subsidiary bank have not been included in the company valuation. The assessment contains three scenar-ios for each of these (Low, Mid and High Case) for both value components (RBI Group excluding Russia and the network bank Russia). In the valuation of the Russian network bank, possible scenarios – ranging from pacification to further escalation – with corresponding probabilities of occurrence and the current restrictions on distributions were also taken into account depending on the further development of the war between Ukraine and Russia. The mid-case scenario rep-resents the expected value of the RBI Group excluding Russia, which is why this scenario was used to calculate the recognised value in use. A conservative weighting of scenarios from the low case was used to determine the value in use of network bank Russia. The discounting of the cash flow that can be achieved with the valuation object was undertaken with the aid of a risk-adequate capitalisation interest rate. For the valuation of the RBI Group excluding Russia, a cost of equity after tax of 9.55% was used (31 December 2025: 9.91%). Any change to capital costs of plus or minus 100 basis points would result in a fall or rise of the established company value of RBI Group by -11.33% or +14.03% respectively. The sustainable growth rate for both value components (RBI Group excluding Russia and the network bank Russia) was set at 2.00% (31 December 2025: 2.00%). The beta factor for the core business was derived from a peer group of internationally active banks with a risk profile comparable to that of RBI but without a significant exposure in Russia. The beta factor for the valuation of the Russian network bank was determined from a peer group of Eastern European local banks. Due in particular to the lower cost of equity and higher earnings forecasts, the value in use improved significantly at 30 June 2026 to EUR 45.90 per share compared with 31 December 2025 (31 December 2025: EUR 37.95 per share). The recoverable amount at 30 June 2026 is the higher of the value derived from a comparison between the value in use and the fair value less costs to sell, and this was the fair value derived from the stock market price less costs to sell. Hedge accounting Fixed interest rate risk positions as part of the ordinary business activities of the Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group result from the conclusion of loans and term deposits with customers as well as from the purchase of securities and from issues. These fixed interest rate risk positions are hedged either by means of micro hedge accounting or a portfolio fair value hedge. In micro hedge accounting, mainly positions on the liabilities side are hedged with regard to their fixed interest rate risk in order to reduce negative maturity transformation effects. Furthermore, on the asset side, there is an increase in interest rate hedging on a micro basis for large-volume customer transactions with stable cash flows and in the securities area. With fair value hedge accounting on a portfolio basis (“portfolio fair value hedge”), interest rate risks at the Raiffeisenland-esbank Oberösterreich Group are managed at the level of three dynamic portfolios. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group’s risk management identifies fixed-interest underlying transactions on the basis of defined criteria and allocates them to the relevant hedge portfolio. The underlying transactions represent fixed-interest loans and securities as well as deposits and liabilities evidenced by certificates in euros in the category “At amortised cost” (AC) (fixed-interest asset portfolio and fixed-interest liability port-folio). These transactions also meet other general criteria (e.g. no underlying transactions in a micro hedge, no defaulted or inter-company transactions). Variable interest instruments in which caps and floors are embedded also have a fixed interest rate risk, at least tempo-rarily, if the figures exceed or fall below the interest rate limits (cap/floor portfolio). Variable financial assets with interest rate floors are accounted for in a separate portfolio. Loans, promissory note loans and securities with explicit floors are allocated to this portfolio currently in compliance with the criteria listed above. Sensitivity information on allowances and provisions in Stages 1 and 2 In accordance with IFRS 9, “forward looking information” – meaning macroeconomic forecasts – is used to calculate the balance sheet allowances and provisions. Based on this, statistical models are used to determine the IFRS 9 risk param-eters and subsequently the balance sheet allowances and provisions. Both the macroeconomic forecasts and the calcu-lated risk parameters are subject to estimation uncertainty in the model. In order to be able to better assess and estimate this uncertainty due to changed parameters, the Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group calculates sensitivity anal-yses of the balance sheet allowances and provisions in Stages 1 and 2 and presents them on the following pages. At the reporting date 30 June 2026, realisations are in use until 2025 for the macroeconomic factors used. These are no longer affected by an HCPI or real estate price shift and therefore remain unchanged for the sensitivity analysis. The shift to the macroeconomic forecasts will take effect from 2026. HCPI shift of +/–2 percentage points: the HCPI is an important macroeconomic indicator from Raiffeisenlandesbank Ober-österreich’s perspective. It was therefore identified as a relevant metric for the sensitivity analysis. The 2 percentage point shift in the annual HCPI growth rate is used to show the sensitivity to the PD risk parameter. A parallel shift is performed on all annual HCPI forecast values. Based on the changed HCPI growth rates, alternative IFRS 9 PDs are determined, which are subsequently used for staging and for the calculation of the allowances and provisions on the balance sheet per shift scenario. The amount of the shift was chosen on the basis of an expert estimate and represents a mean change in the risk parameters. Changes in parameters were presented as a shift in the GDP growth rate of +/–1 percentage point at 31 December 2025, rather than in the HCPI growth rate. The change was made in response to the growing importance of the harmonised consumer price index. Real estate price shift +/-5% points: The fluctuation of the residential and commercial property price growth rate is the central explanatory factor in the IFRS 9 LGD models of Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich and was therefore identified as a relevant metric for the sensitivity analysis. Specifically, both the current projected residential and commercial property price growth rate per year and the residential and commercial real estate securities are reduced or increased by 5 per-centage points. This results in an indirect shift of the IFRS 9 LGD and thus an increased or reduced balance sheet allow-ances and provisions. Furthermore, the real estate securities for each account are reduced or increased by 5 percentage points in absolute terms for the purposes of the sensitivity analysis. The amount the shifts was chosen on the basis of an expert estimate and represents a mean change in the risk parameters. Principles of risk management The long-term success of Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group is largely dependent upon active risk management. In order to achieve this target, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich, as the dominant group company, has implemented risk management with structures that facilitate the identification and measurement of all risks in the Group in accordance with sections 39, 39a, Austrian Banking Act and the Credit Institution Risk Management Regulation (KI-RMV) (credit risks, equity risks, liquidity risks, market risks, macroeconomic risks, operational risks and other risks) and their active managerial counteraction. Credit, investment and operational risk are managed by RMKM (Risk Management Credit, Reporting, Op-erational Risk), while liquidity, market and macroeconomic risk are managed by RMIM (Risk Management ICAAP & Market Risk). ESG (environment, social, governance) risks, as the latest dimension of risks, were integrated into the existing risk categories, with the greatest focus remaining on climate and environmental risks – in part because social and governance risks have not been classified as material. To this end, inputs in the form of metrics and scores are provided centrally by a unit that is organisationally assigned to RMIM. The Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich in general only aims its work at business areas in which it has the requisite expertise in the assessment of the specific risks. The inclusion of new business areas or products is preceded by an appropriate analysis of the business-specific risks. Risk Controlling analyses all risks and examines adherence to the defined risk limits by means of ongoing variance anal-yses. Internal/Group Audit assesses the effectiveness of working procedures, processes and internal controls. 7.1.2. Integration of climate and environmental risks in risk management Climate and environmental risks form part of the risk inventory of existing risk categories. The relevant risk area is therefore responsible for measurement and reporting - creating the parameters, metrics and resulting analyses that serve as input, as well as the general transfer of expertise, are carried out by a central unit within risk management. The annual risk inventory enables changes in financial materiality to be recognised and, if necessary, measures (e.g. increased monitoring) to be derived. The traditional risk committees are ultimately served automatically by integrating climate and environmental risks into the existing risk categories. Climate and environmental risks are analysed in two dimensions for risk management purposes. These are represented by temporary and physical climate and environmental risks. Accordingly, these dimensions are considered separately. Specific metrics are required in each case here to enable the measurability and therefore the assessment of the different aspects of climate and environmental risks. Transitory climate and environmental risks Transitory climate risk is the term used to describe financial losses that may occur directly or indirectly as a result of adapting to or failing to adapt to a lower-carbon and more environmentally sustainable economy. The transmission channel thus results, for example, from technical progress, changes in market regulations and preferences or the increasing and rising pricing of greenhouse gas emissions. In addition to climate risks, changes in the environment due to external influences can also lead to transitory risks. Com-panies have a strong influence on ecosystem services as part of their own business activities. The risks for companies (and the associated transmission channel) can arise, on the one hand, from regulations but also from taxes and levies (e.g. for water consumption, pollution, land utilisation). Interim Financial Report 2026 87 The Group IFRS consolidated interim financial statements 2026 | Notes to the consolidated financial statements | Risk report The Group Interim Financial Report 2026 | Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements 87 Physical climate and environmental risks Essentially, physical climate risks relate to the more frequent (change in probability) and more intense (level of damage) occurrence of extreme weather events and natural hazards. In order to assess the materiality for the Bank, it is necessary to consider physical risks from two perspectives. On the one hand, physical risks differ geographically based on the pre-dicted change in each region, and the question of “Where is financing provided?” must therefore be clarified. On the other hand, such events can have a strong impact on a wide range of corporate activities. The transmission channel thus results, for example, from additional costs or disruptions to operations (caused by extreme weather events or natural hazards) as well as supply chain bottlenecks or a business model risk. In addition to climate risks, changes in the environment due to external influences can also lead to potential financial risks. Changes in natural capital (e.g. water and soil) can have serious impacts on sectors or businesses that depend on certain ecosystem services. Severely affected sectors or businesses are likely to suffer losses if they cannot access necessary ecosystem services to the extent to which they are accustomed. The transmission channel thus arises from a reduced ecosystem service because the required natural capital is not available in sufficient quantities or not (or no longer) in the required quality. Scenarios and time horizons As part of the risk inventory, different scenarios and time horizons are taken into account when assessing climate and environmental risks by risk type. A materiality assessment was carried out for each scenario and each selected time horizon using standardised matrices (scenarios and time horizons). The risk types use metrics tailored to the dimensions (e.g. scores, simulated PD shifts) as a basis for this, which are then applied qualitatively or quantitatively by the risk types, taking into account the different scenarios and time horizons. The results for each risk type are shown in the tables below. The NGFS scenarios (Network for Greening the Financial System) described below were used as scenarios for climate risks: The “Orderly Transition” scenario is based on the assumption that climate policy actions are introduced at an early stage and tightened on a continuous basis. Both transitory and physical risks are limited in the short term. Over the 2030 and 2040 time horizons, business models that have not invested in decarbonisation will be increasingly faced with higher costs and the resulting consequences. The physical consequences of climate change increase until 2030 due to the early intro-duction and ongoing tightening of climate change mitigation actions, but this acceleration will slow down by 2040 and the consequences will therefore not become more frequent/intensive (compared to 2030). A high transition risk arises in the “Disorderly Transition” scenario due to delayed or different policies in countries and/or sectors. Delayed action e.g. results in a (necessary) abrupt increase in the price of CO2. This in turn puts too much of a strain on many business models that are heavily affected by rising CO2 prices, especially up to 2040, and for which the high price increase is not economically viable. The development of the physical consequences of climate change in the “Disorderly” scenario is, in fact, the same as the one for the “Orderly Transition”. In the “Hothouse World” scenario, it is assumed that climate policy actions will be implemented in some countries, but that global efforts will not be sufficient to stop significant global warming. The consequences of this are increasingly high physical risks over the various time horizons, which have irreversible consequences for society and the economy. Two scenarios are considered with regard to environmental risks, for which an internal elaboration based on the NGFS scenarios was carried out. The “business as usual” scenario assumes that no major (political) efforts are made to protect natural capital. Companies can therefore consume and, in many cases, overconsume, the resources they need, such as water and land. The first impact can therefore be expected by 2030, while many resources will no longer be available in the required form by 2040, resulting in high costs. These in turn mean that some business models will no longer function in their original form. Credit risk The credit risk constitutes the risk to the bank that a loss will occur as a result of the non-fulfilment of the contractual obligations of customers or contracting partners. The credit risk results mainly from loans and advances to customers and banks and from securities from the banking book. Credit risk comprises the following sub-categories: counterparty or credit risk, securitisation risk, concentration risks (con-centration risk relating to individual borrowers, sector distribution, country risk, foreign currency loans and repayment instruments) and CVA risk. Climate and environmental risks are quantified within the credit risk framework using stress scenarios as part of the integrated stress test. The risk is communicated through the key risk figure for “unexpected loss”. For credit ratings higher than 10A, the calculation is carried out using MSCI’s CreditMan-ager programme. The risks and opportunities from loan defaults or changes in creditworthiness are determined using a market valuation model. The risk for default classes 10A to 10C is calculated separately. Unsecured portions of exposures for which no specific provision has been made are allocated to the unexpected loss. An LGD of 67.0% is applied for retail customers, and an LGD of 39.4% for corporate customers (Best Estimation of Expected Loss (BEEL)). The loan portfolio is analysed – broken down by IFRS segments, specific industries, ratings or rating models, NACE sectors and regions – and reported to the Managing Board on a monthly basis. Credit risk concentrations are identified by analysing each borrower or group of borrowers. In addition, the counterparty risk report provides quarterly or ad hoc reporting on credit risk to the Managing Board. For the purposes of the group’s risk reporting, it takes into account all elements of credit risk related to loans and advances, such as individual debtor default risk, country and sector risks. pricing (including taxes, levies and penalties) of harmful greenhouse gases or other negative environmental impacts. Among other things, this tax-induced steering effect leads to changes in relative prices (depending on the amount), which in turn has a direct impact on companies’ business models, financial performance and consequently their credit ratings. Consequently, the analysis of these effects and the portfolio’s exposure to them plays a key role in assessing transitory risks within credit risk. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich identifies these risk indicators at an early stage by incorporating climate and environmental risks via Climate and Environ-ment Transitional Risk Scores as part of its risk inventory. Equity investment risk Equity investment risk refers to the potential risk of a future impairment in the value of equity investments. Equity invest-ment risk comprises several types of sub-risk, some of which are interdependent and are therefore intertwined. The most significant risks in this regard are the risk of dividend default, the risk of current value depreciation, the risk arising from the reduction of hidden reserves, macroeconomic risks at the level of the equity investment (cash flows and capitalisation rates), and the risk arising from industry concentrations. The Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Group has a broadly diversified equity investment portfolio. A value-at-risk model is used to assess the risk potential from equity investments, which calculates statically significant iterations based on these external expert valuations (generally expert values based on the discounted cash flow) and subsequently deter-mines the corresponding risk potential for the economic perspective (99.9%) by comparing the calculated value-at-risk values (confidence interval: 99.9%) with the expert value for each participating interest. Historical fluctuation intensities observed in the market with regards to cash flow volatilities (of the underlying industry) and discount rates are applied to the input parameters used in the expert valuation procedure; and statistically significant iterations are thus calculated. The procedure is similar for proportional values of listed participations. The risk potential of the entire equity investment portfolio can thus be determined by aggregating the risk potential of all equity investments. Based on the existing external valuations (market capitalisation or appraiser ratings at the end of the relevant financial period), the risk potential from investments is quantified using a simulation model. The spread of the net result from valu-ation of equity investments is determined on the basis of a Monte Carlo simulation depending on fluctuating input factors, in accordance with their historical volatility. The outcome is a distribution of probabilities for the individual equity investment values. This can then be used to determine the potential risk for the equity investments and thus for the entire equity investment portfolio. In addition to qualitative analyses of data quality and model design, the validation of the equity investment risk model includes above all backtesting. This involves checking whether the risk potential forecast by the model adequately covers both book value and market value losses. The operative business activities of the investments are closely monitored by sending members of the board at Raiffeisen-landesbank Oberösterreich to Managing Boards, Supervisory Boards, and other committees. Periodic equity investment risk management includes the analysis and testing of financial statements and planning figures. From the perspective of equity investment risk, geopolitical conflicts (Russia-Ukraine, Middle East), volatilities in relation to US tariff policy and changes in inflation and interest rate expectations posed risks for companies in the investment portfolio throughout 2025. The first half of 2026 was marked by an unexpected shock (the war with Iran). Increased volatility was observed in the cost structure in the case of energy-intensive portfolio companies (AMAG, voestalpine), and the conflict led to growing planning uncertainties. Transitory climate and environmental risks Multiple transitional risks could arise in relation to equity investments along the corresponding value chain (intermediate products, production, end products). This gives rise to financial risks for equity investments as a result of bans on end products, more onerous regulatory requirements or additional taxation for the end consumer, which may make products considerably more expensive (e.g. stricter emissions standards for cars). If these political measures lead to a fall in demand for the (end) products manufac-tured by the equity investment, this will expose the company to corresponding risks. Physical climate and environmental risks Physical risks are financial risks arising directly from the adverse effects of climate and environmental change on the relevant investment. The acute physical vulnerabilities, in the form of natural disasters resulting from global warming (e.g. floods, landslides, etc.), are primarily concentrated in the industrial investments and the real estate sector of the equity investment portfolio. Interest rate risk management Interest rate risk management at Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich is carried out on the basis of management strate-gies agreed with the Managing Board as a whole and financial targets. The interest rate projections and the respective concerted positioning are continuously presented within the framework of the Asset Liability Committee. At the consoli-dated level, the aim is to achieve a fixed-interest surplus in order to capture maturity transformation outcomes in future. Interest rate risk is managed primarily through underlying transactions (loans, issues) or their hedging. For asset items in proprietary fond holdings, a “statement of financial position review” is carried out; the bonds contained within the fund thus enter into the hedging strategies of the consolidated banking book. Underlying business transactions can be classified as fair value option in order to reduce the statement of financial position fair value risk of the overall position. For this purpose, however, a partial or full hedging transaction must exist for this underlying transaction. It is also possible to link several underlying transactions with one hedging transaction if the busi-ness content is almost identical. An explicit increase in the interest rate risk of the FVPL position by including a transaction in the fair value option is avoided. In addition to hedges at the individual level of Assets and Liabilities in the form of hedge accounting, Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich manages interest rate risks at the macro level within the framework of the application of the “portfolio fair value hedge”. Both fixed-interest assets and liabilities in defined maturity bands are combined into an overall risk position and hedged with corresponding derivative hedging transactions. It should be noted that variable instruments in which caps/floors are embedded also have fixed interest rate risks. The bottom layer approach is applied in accordance with the EU carve-out regulations on IAS 39. Stressed balance sheet allowances and provisions are simulated based on the pessimistic scenario from IFRS 9. The result is increased allowances and provisions due to the increased PDs and LGDs from this pessimistic scenario and the resulting increased stage transfers from Stage 1 to 2. The difference between the stressed allowances and provisions from the pessimistic scenario and the booked allowances and provisions results in the macroeconomic risk pillar 2. This amount is taken into account in the economic perspective (99.9%) of the risk-bearing capacity analysis as a deduction item in the cover assets and thus increases the risk utilisation. For the pessimistic scenario, depending on the direction of impact of the macroeconomic factor, the upper or lower just under 80% to 90% quantile (or 20% to 10% quantile) of the forecast interval is used by means of a polynomial function. This reflects the rising uncertainty with an increasing forecast horizon. See Note “1.3. Management judgement and esti-mates” for further details on the macroeconomic forecasts used. 7.2.4. Operational risk Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich defines operational risk as the risk of loss caused by the inappropriateness or failure of internal processes, people or systems, or caused by external events. Operational risk includes legal and reputation risks. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich uses the standardised measurement approach (SMA) to quantify operational risk as part of its overall bank risk management. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich uses both organisational measures and IT systems to limit this type of risk as far as possible. A high degree of security is attained by means of limit systems, competence regulations, a risk-adequate internal control system, a comprehensive security manual as a code of conduct and directive, as well as scheduled and unsched-uled audits by Internal Audit. The operative management of this type of risk involves risk discussions and analyses with managers (early warning system). And the systematic recording of errors in a database for analysis (ex-post analysis). The Non-Financial Risk Committee (NFRC) was established in 2023 as an interface committee for various specialist de-partments relating to non-financial risk. Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich has its own Legal department in order to minimise and hedge against legal risks at a qualitative level. This department deals with operational legal issues, including in particular the drafting of contracts that are certain in law, monitoring current developments in case law, ongoing legal advice for the Bank’s operational business areas and managing legal disputes in and out of court. As part of the compliance organisation of Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich, the BWG Compliance Team acts as a second-line function for monitoring compliance with legal provisions by Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich, its executive bodies and its employees using suitable tools. Raiffeisenlandes-bank Oberösterreich has a press office for press relations and dealing with negative publicity (reputation risk). Transitory climate and environmental risks are also processed accordingly in the operational risk management tools (assessments, stress tests, loss database, regular reporting). Fraud management, as a cross-functional task within Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich, follows the approach that the central Fraud Officer assumes overall responsibility and thereby coordinates activities across specialist departments. The experts in each of these departments are generally responsible the products and processes within their area of expertise and thus also for targeted implementation measures and the ongoing flow of information to the Fraud Officer. Fraud man-agement – as part of the second-line function – also reports to the NFRC. The current geopolitical situation, such as the US tariff policy, does not at present have any direct impact on the operational risks faced by Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich. However, it cannot be ruled out that unforeseeable future events may influence the operational risk. Risk-bearing capacity analysis The risk-bearing capacity analysis compares the aggregated overall bank risk of the CRR Group of Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich, organised by credit risks, market risks, equity investment risks, refinancing risks (as a measurement pa-rameter for liquidity risk), operational risks, and other risks to risk coverage. This comparison of the risks with the available coverage depicts the risk-bearing capacity from an economic perspective (99.9%). The cover fund from the economic perspective (99.9%) is composed of equity, hidden reserves/liabilities and deductible items. The deduction items take into account macroeconomic risk and climate risks, among other things. This comparison enables Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich to guarantee that it can cover unexpected losses from its own funds without major negative effects. Economic capital serves as a risk measure for calculating unexpected losses. It is defined as the minimum amount of capital necessary to cover unexpected losses with a probability of 99.9% within one year. In accordance with the “ECB Guidelines for the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP)”, Raiffeisen-landesbank Oberösterreich distinguishes between the economic perspective (99.9%) and the supplementary normative perspective: the economic view focuses on a present value risk assessment and utilisation of the risk cover funds, whereas the normative view focuses on statement of financial position risks in the income statement and their impact on the regu-latory capital ratios. Stress tests In addition to the isolated stress tests covering all risk types, various scenarios are simulated in the integrated stress test and their impact on risk utilisation is presented. Furthermore, in the normative perspective of the ICAAP, several defined scenarios are simulated and their impact on the regulatory capital ratios is examined. Impact on risk-bearing capacity from an economic perspective (99.9%) The objective is to analyse, from an economic point of view, the risk-bearing capacity under stress conditions for all types of risk and the risk coverage and to determine the respective risk utilisation. The calculation of stressed credit risk is carried out by simulating rating downgrades of individual borrowers operating in an industry significant to Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich, which has a strong negative outlook. In addition to the rating downgrade, a reduction in securities is simulated. Moreover, in the area of credit risk, the impact of spread changes on the exposure and the associated risk is taken into account. The stressed equity investment risk is determined using the ROBert simulation tool (Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich Equity Investment Risk Tool) on the basis of stressed input parameters (e.g. cash flow profitability). In the area of market risk, interest rate and credit spread risk are subjected to stress testing. Upon adjusted interest rates and spreads, the present value of the portfolio is recalculated. The change in present value resulting from the interest rate spread shift has a direct impact on the risk covering potential. As part of liquidity risk management, the scenarios defined by the Austrian Raiffeisen Protection Scheme (Öster-reichischen Raiffeisen-Sicherungseinrichtung – ÖRS) “Reputation Crisis”, “Systemic Crisis” and “Problem Case” – are simulated and the resulting refinancing risk is determined. In the case of a reputation crisis, the critical situation is based on damage to the Raiffeisen name or reputation in any form. The resulting consequences are mapped in the reputation crisis model. The systemic crisis scenario reflects a broader market crisis, irrespective of whether Raiffeisen itself is directly affected by a specific crisis situation. The problem case is a combination of the two isolated crisis cases. The modelling largely reflects a combination of these crisis scenarios. In terms of operational risk, the total simulated default amount of the n-largest borrowers and the occurrence of the n-largest loss events can be simulated. Furthermore, it is possible to simulate other scenarios, such as the Iran conflict, a US tariff scenario, the war in Ukraine or the 2008 financial crisis. In addition, scenarios regarding climate and environmental risks are already being integrated into the stress test frame-work. Currently, the focus is on transitory climate risks, which arise primarily from changing political and legal framework conditions. The NGFS scenarios (Orderly, Disorderly, Hot House – 2030, 2040, 2050 respectively) are used as the basis for climate stress tests at Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich. The results of the scenarios are derived from CGE (Com-putable General Equilibrium) modelling, which uses the respective NGFS scenario metrics as shock parameters. The resulting stressed probabilities of default per customer or sector are subsequently used to simulate specific credit risk indicators, such as, for example, for the balance sheet allowances and provisions in accordance with IFRS 9 (expected credit loss), for the 99.9% unexpected loss and for the RWAs. It is also possible to simulate a physical climate risk as well as the loss of the customers with the highest GHG emissions. It is also possible to analyse the impact of defined recovery options. The quantification of the catalogue of measures in the ICAAP is updated annually on the basis of Raiffeisenlandesbank Oberösterreich’s recovery plan; the measures are therefore based on the recovery options in the recovery plan. To evaluate the qualifications of an applicant for public employment or to review the performance of a public employee – RCW 42.30.110 (g); Adjournment Clallam County Fire District 3 Motto: Serve, Respect, Prevent and Protect Meeting Minutes (10.20.2026) Page 1 of 4 BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS – MEETING MINUTES October 20, 2026 Chairman Miano called the Board of Commissioners Meeting for Clallam County Fire District 3 to order at 1:00 p.m. via the Zoom App and in person at 255 Carlsborg Road in Sequim. Present were: Commissioners Bill Miano, and Jeff Nicholas, Fire Chief Justin Grider, Deputy Chief Tony Hudson, Finance Manager Misty Shaw, District Secretary Lori Coleman, Battalion Chief Stefanie Anderson, Human Resource Manager Charles Clarke, Firefighter/Paramedics Brent Lovell and Erik Payne, and Maintenance Supervisor Tharin Huisman, Online were: Commissioner Mike Mingee, Admin Assistant Caity Karapostoles, Volunteer Coordinator Chris Lovering, Captains Travis Anderson, Marc Lawson and Kolby Konopaski, Firefighter/Paramedic Bryce McGinley, Firefighter/EMT Libby Swanberg, Facilities Technician John Brygider, Mechanics Steve Phillips and Brad Schroeder, reporter Matt Nash, anonymous, and citizen Joel McKeen. Changes to the Agenda – After discussion about this being a very large agenda and potentially tabling topics to save time, there were no agenda changes made. PUBLIC COMMENT – None. CONSENT AGENDA 1.) Regular Meeting Minutes, October 6th, 2026 2.) Volunteer Pay - $$32,585.00 3.) Claims Accounts Payable Claim check numbers 114097 through 114139 dated October 20, 2026, totaling $182,327.23; Payroll EFTs and IRS Deposit for Monthly Payroll dated October 9, 2026, totaling $981,219.21 for a disbursement grand total equaling $1,163,546.44. Commissioner Miano moved, and Commissioner Nicholas seconded, to approve the Consent Agenda as presented. MOTION CARRIED. Next Meetings – November 2nd, 2026 – Special Board Meeting November 3rd, 2026 – Regular Board Meeting – Chief Grider will attend remotely. Pre-Authorizing Commissioner Activities – Commissioner Mingee and Nicholas will attend the WFCA Conference in Spokane this week. GOOD OF THE ORDER – Chief Grider reported – • With the recent line-staff vacancies, he intends to promote a captain to a captain floater position beginning January 1, 2027. Interviews have been conducted, and an appointment is pending. Board of Commissioners Meeting Minutes Meeting Minutes (10.20.2026) Page 2 of 4 Battalion Chief Reports– Battalion Chief Anderson reported – • Attended a Battalion Chief, an Operations, and a Commissioner meeting in September. • Battalion Chiefs continue to backfill staffing as necessary and fill the upstaffing positions. • Ten training requests were submitted and approved; arrangements for these classes are ongoing. • Continues to work on scheduling quarterly training for career and volunteers with VC Lovering. • Probationary members continue to progress on their task books across all shifts. • Firefighting testing was held on the 17th and 18th of September. Twenty-two candidates were tested, and fifteen of those were invited to the Chief’s Interviews. The District has offered five conditional offers to those who were successful. The testing required twenty-one evaluators and support staff. • The transition continues to the Blue Card program. All captains and some acting captains have completed the online coursework, and a few captains/battalion chiefs recently completed the three-day IC Course. This training is ongoing. • Preparations for training in 2027 are underway. Agenda Bill 1: Station 31 CUP and Design – Commissioner Mingee presented the attached proposal for professional services, preliminary site drawings, and estimated costs for a Conditional Use Permit (CUP) for the property on Gold Dust Lane for a new Station 31. Commissioner Mingee also stated that he wants to continue research and discussions regarding Station 32 upgrades, stating that DC Hudson and Maintenance Supervisor Huisman are aware of the work to be completed. Commissioner Miano moved, and Commissioner Nicholas seconded, to approve spending $68,000 to fund the CUP design for Gold Dust Lane property for a potential new Station 31. MOTION CARRIED. Agenda Bill 2: Vehicle Replacement Plan Presentation - Maintenance Supervisor Tharin Huisman presented an Apparatus Replacement Plan, including an overview of the current fleet, replacement guidelines established by AP Triton and NFPA 1910, funding needs, and proposed apparatus purchases for 2027 and 2028. He advised against refurbishing apparatus that are 18 years or older, noting that while refurbishment may initially cost less than purchasing new or used equipment, the remaining service life is uncertain and represents a significant risk. He also noted that replacement parts for several older apparatus are difficult, if not nearly impossible, to obtain. Finance Manager Misty Shaw reviewed the 2027 budget request, which currently includes $750,480 to replace one tender and one ambulance, and transfer remaining funds for future fleet purchases. She stated that the presentation illustrates how far behind the District is in updating its fleet. Using AP Triton’s point-based evaluation scale, which recommends replacement at 28 points, the District has apparatus rated as high as 72 points. Commissioners requested that the plan be returned for further discussion when additional time is available, potentially during a special meeting. Commissioner Mingee stated that the proposed 2027 funding amount appears reasonable but that he is not prepared to make decisions regarding replacements beyond 2027 at this time. INFORMATION ONLY. NO ACTION TAKEN. Agenda Bill 3: US101 Simdars Interchange Project – Chief Grider reported that the interchange at Simdars Road has been identified by the City of Sequim and Washington Department of Transportation as incomplete from the previous project. He reported that Phase I of the project was completed and Phase II was to finish the westbound and eastbound exit/entry ramps and construct a frontage road connecting Happy Board of Commissioners Meeting Minutes Meeting Minutes (10.20.2026) Page 3 of 4 Valley Road and Palo Alto Road. The new initiative being pursued is to separate Phase II into two phases and emphasize completing the interchange project while placing the frontage road into the final phase. The District identified this area in the Capital Improvement Plan for an eastside fire station, and the Chief has been supportive of this project. Chief Grider is seeking concurrence from the Board to continue partnering with these agencies to ensure that this is a priority; the Board concurs. INFORMATION ONLY. NO ACTION TAKEN. Agenda Bill 4: Fire Chief Vacancy – Chief Grider reported that at the September 15th, 2026, board meeting, he informed the Board that he does not intend to renew his contract. He will finish the contract term and asked the Board to direct staff with recruitment expectations. The Board reported that they will work with the Human Resource Manager to update the job description, posting, etc. for impending recruitment efforts for the position. INFORMATION ONLY. NO ACTION TAKEN. Agenda Bill 5: 3Q 2026 Financial Reports – Finance Manger Misty Shaw reported that General and EMS property tax revenue is on track. At this time of year, the District usually receives about 63% of its yearly tax revenue. The increase from last year is mainly due to the levy lid lift. Grant revenue includes a $23,600 Washington DNR Wildfire Risk Reduction and Prevention grant. Timber sale revenue was higher than expected but the County is projecting no timber revenue for 2027. Ambulance service revenue is up 58% from last year because of payment timing, higher transport rates, and favorable changes to the Olympic Ambulance contract. Overall revenue is meeting expectations. Expenses are also generally on track, although some areas are higher than last year. Increased costs include election-related commissioner expenses; legal, technology, and other administrative services; overtime, wages, benefits, protective gear, and resident transport billing credit in Suppression and EMS; Fire Code Technician hours and grant-funded prevention purchases; wildland deployment costs; and the use of CERT donation funds. Vehicle costs increased due to enterprise services, fuel, wages, and benefit costs, while facility costs increased slightly. All other expense categories were reviewed, and no major concerns were identified. FM Shaw showed two graphs through September 30th, 2026: one was for revenue and the other was for expenditures; the graphs primarily showed that 91% of revenue is due to property tax collection and the majority of the expenditures are from fire suppression and EMS. INFORMATION ONLY. NO ACTION TAKEN. Commissioner Miano called for an 8-minute break at 2:25, returning at 2:30. Agenda Bill 6: Budget Workshop – 2027 Draft Proposed Budget – Finance Manager Misty Shaw presented the draft 2027 budget. She briefly reviewed the 2027 revenue forecast, noting that the largest percentage change was in the Grant Fund line item due to the HazMat Grant that is expected to be received in 2027. She noted that there are increases in Charges for services that are primarily due to mechanic services and wildland deployments. Ambulance services revenue increased by 150% to reflect current activity and increased rates. Miscellaneous categories showed a 25% reduction largely due to the decrease in investment interest. She added that the general levy rate will be $1.50 in 2027; the CPI inflator that was built into the levy of 4.5% was not realized because of the $1.50 cap and relatively flat assessed property values. She noted that there are no new staff added to the budget for 2027, although one position will be changed in rank when the captain floater position is filled. The board discussed the 2027 draft budget as presented and asked that staff add an area that budgets for fees and fines, keep the 4% apparatus replacement budget, and include 2.7% of property tax revenue to be used for capital. Commissioner Mingee added that he believes the fundamental structural problem for the district relies solely on the service delivery model and he expects to see significant change in 2027. INFORMATION ONLY. NO ACTION TAKEN.
